question: What are the best tools and libraries for rendering and generating Gaussian splats in web-based 3D scenes? Focus on the PlayCanvas ecosystem and surrounding open-source tools that enable fast rendering and generation — ideally covering the full workflow from capture/generation to web display. Target is a SvelteKit web app using WebGPU.
executive_summary: PlayCanvas Engine (v2.17.2, MIT) is the most production-ready WebGPU Gaussian splat renderer, with a full ecosystem from capture to web display via the SOG format (95% size reduction over PLY). However, no off-the-shelf library supports injecting an external GPUDevice, meaning integration into an existing WebGPU render loop requires adopting a full engine, forking a research implementation, or using multi-canvas CSS compositing. The open-source training pipeline (COLMAP + gsplat, Apache 2.0) is mature and matches proprietary quality within 1 dB PSNR. AI-based generation is limited to single-object prototyping and not production-ready for environments.

key_findings.finding: PlayCanvas Engine offers the most complete WebGPU Gaussian splat stack: SplatTransform CLI, SuperSplat editor, GSplatComponent runtime with LOD streaming, and the SOG format achieving 95% size reduction.
All production-grade lightweight splat libraries (gsplat.js, Spark, GaussianSplats3D) are WebGL-only; no library supports injecting an external WebGPU GPUDevice.

Four compositing strategies exist for integrating splats with an existing WebGPU scene, ranging from same-pass rendering (simplest) to depth pre-pass (full interpenetration), with multi-canvas CSS as the lowest-change option.
gsplat (Apache 2.0) is the recommended trainer: fastest (20 min RTX 3060), lowest VRAM (4 GB), and within 0.3 dB PSNR of the non-commercially-licensed INRIA original.

AI-based Gaussian splat generation is functional for single-object prototyping (TRELLIS) but not production-ready for scenes; TRELLIS 2 dropped Gaussian output, suggesting industry trend away from generative 3DGS.

open_questions: What is PlayCanvas engine's bundle size overhead when used solely for splat rendering alongside an existing WebGPU renderer?
Is PlayCanvas Unified Splat Rendering (beta) stable enough for production use?
Can a minimal WebGPU splat renderer be built in ~500 lines WGSL+TS to accept an external GPUDevice?
Will SPZ format achieve glTF standardization, and should it be targeted over SOG?
Does Spark work with Three.js's experimental WebGPU renderer?
contradictions: TRELLIS is the best AI-to-3DGS tool, but TRELLIS 2 dropped Gaussian output entirely -- the industry may be moving away from generative Gaussian splats toward generative meshes.
